questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Zero flux through a closed surface
questions.learningObjective: Refute the claim that every closed surface has zero net flux
questions.stem: A colleague claims that a closed surface always has zero net flux because it is closed. Which field shows the claim to be false, with the box running from 0 to 1 in each coordinate?

options.text: F(x,y,z) = (x, 0, 0) has divergence 1, so its net flux through the box is 1, not zero.
No field can refute the claim, because a closed surface always encloses a net-zero flux.
options.misconception: repeats the false claim as its own refutation

options.text: F(x,y,z) = (x, minus x, 0) is divergence free everywhere, so it confirms the claim instead.
options.misconception: misses that the second component does not depend on y

options.text: F(x,y,z) = (x, y, z) is divergence free everywhere, so it confirms the claim instead.
options.misconception: believes a radial field has zero divergence

questions.explanation: The divergence of this field is 1, so the divergence theorem gives a total flux of 1 through the unit box, which contradicts the claim. A radial field has divergence 3 and refutes it too.
questions.hint: Look for a field whose divergence is a nonzero constant.

questions.learningObjective: Justify the flux through a plate using a projected area
questions.stem: A log entry records a uniform field of strength 4 passing through a flat circular plate of radius 2 whose normal makes a 60 degree angle with the field, and the recorded flux is 8 pi. Which reasoning makes that entry correct?

options.text: The flux equals the field strength times the full disk area, 4 times 4 pi.
options.misconception: ignores the angle between the plate and the field

options.text: The flux equals the field strength times the disk area times the cosine of the 60 degree angle.
The flux equals the field strength times the disk area times the sine of the angle.
options.misconception: uses sine where the cosine is required

options.text: The flux equals the field strength times the disk area times the tangent of the angle.
options.misconception: uses a tangent ratio for a projection

questions.explanation: The plate's area is 4 pi, and the field contributes the cosine of 60 degrees, which is one half, so the flux is 8 pi. Using the sine instead would give a larger and wrong value.
questions.hint: Project the disk onto the plane across the field.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compare the flux carried by two patches with different orientations
questions.stem: A dome-shaped observatory shutter is drawn in the log: patch P lies flat on the top of the dome where the field is perpendicular to the surface, and patch Q lies on the sloping side where the field makes a 60 degree angle with the outward normal. Both patches have area 2 square metres and the field magnitude is 4. Which statement compares the flux through the two patches correctly?

options.text: Patch P carries no flux because the field there is perpendicular rather than parallel to the surface.
options.misconception: thinks a perpendicular field means zero flux

options.text: Both patches carry the same flux because they have the same area and the same field magnitude.
options.misconception: ignores the angle between field and normal

options.text: Patch P carries 8 units of flux while patch Q carries 4, so P carries twice as much.
Patch P carries 4 units of flux while patch Q carries 8, since the tilted patch presents more area.
options.misconception: believes tilted patches always catch more field

questions.explanation: Flux is F cos of the angle times the area, so patch P gives 8 and patch Q gives 4. Equal areas and equal field magnitudes do not equalize flux, because the angles differ.
questions.hint: Insert the cosine of each patch's angle to the normal.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Define degeneracy of a surface parametrization
questions.stem: A colleague asks what it means for a surface parametrization to be degenerate, and proposes r of u and v equal to u, v, u v over the unit square as an example. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Degenerate means the map is not one-to-one, so any two-to-one map such as this one is degenerate.
options.misconception: confuses degeneracy with a failure to be injective

options.text: Degenerate means the surface has curvature, so the curved map here is a degenerate example.
options.misconception: equates curvature with degeneracy

options.text: Degenerate means the parametrization fails to be differentiable, which happens whenever z depends on u.
options.misconception: treats any smooth dependence as a derivative failure

options.text: Degenerate means the cross product of the partials vanishes somewhere, and this map stays regular.

questions.explanation: Degeneracy is the vanishing of the cross product of the partials somewhere. For this map the cross product is (-v,-u,1), whose third component keeps it nonzero everywhere.
questions.hint: Check whether the cross product can ever be the zero vector.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a double covering doubles the computed area
questions.stem: A colleague asks why a double-covered chart gives a surface area twice too large instead of leaving the area unchanged. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The area element counts each piece of surface once per covering, so two coverings double the total.
The area element changes sign on the second pass, so the absolute value undoes the effect.
options.misconception: believes signs cancel a double cover

options.text: The area element is unchanged, but the integral runs over a rectangle of twice the area.
options.misconception: blames the rectangle size rather than the covering

options.text: The area element grows with the number of coverings, so the doubling is a geometric effect.
options.misconception: claims the element itself scales with covering

questions.explanation: The area element measures the local stretch of the map, and a double covering presents every piece of surface twice, so the integral accumulates two contributions per piece.
questions.hint: Think about what the element measures locally.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the net flux of a field with nonzero divergence
questions.stem: A log model uses the field F(x,y,z) = (x, minus x, 0) and a colleague asks for the net flux through the box that runs from minus 1 to 1 in each coordinate. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: The net flux is 0, because the second component cancels the first wherever they appear.
options.misconception: assumes opposite components cancel everywhere

options.text: The net flux is 8, because the divergence is 1 and the box has volume 8.
The net flux is 4, because only the face at x = 1 carries an outward component.
options.misconception: keeps only the positive face in the count

options.text: The net flux is 2, because the divergence must be integrated over the area, not the volume.
options.misconception: confuses the volume integral with an area integral

questions.explanation: The divergence is 1 plus 0 plus 0, which is 1, and the box has volume 8, so the net flux is 8. The two components do not cancel, because the second one depends on x rather than on y.
questions.hint: Compute the divergence and multiply by the volume 8.

The mass is 60 grams, because the four densities already account for the whole chart.
options.misconception: sums densities and ignores the areas

questions.explanation: Each square of the chart measures 10 by 12.5 centimetres, so its area is 125 square centimetres, and the densities sum to 60. The mass is therefore 125 times 60, which is 7500 grams.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute the length of the vector area element of a graph
questions.stem: A log model describes a chart surface as the graph z equals f of x and y over a region of the xy-plane, with f x equal to 2 and f y equal to 3 at the point being measured. What is the length of the upward vector area element per unit projected area at that point?
questions.explanation: The factor is the length of the cross product of the partials, root 1 plus f x squared plus f y squared, which here is root 14, about 3.74. A position vector is not the area element.
questions.hint: Take the length of the cross product of the partials.

questions.learningObjective: Detect a double sweep of a cylinder wall in a parameter range
questions.stem: A log model uses r of theta and z equal to 2 cos theta, 2 sin theta, z with theta from 0 to 4 pi and z from 0 to 3. Stage 1: evaluate the surface-area integral over that rectangle. Stage 2: compare it with the true wall area. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: The flux is 0, because a closed surface bounds a region and therefore traps no net field.
options.misconception: believes closed surfaces always carry zero net flux

options.text: The flux is 3, because the divergence is 3 and the volume of the cube is 1.
The flux is 1, because only the face at x = 1 has a nonzero normal component of the field.

questions.explanation: The divergence of this radial field is 3 and the volume is 1, so the total flux is 3. Closedness guarantees a well-defined outward normal, not a vanishing flux.

options.misconception: halves the angular range and keeps the wrong answer

options.text: The surface density must be squared because mass scales with density over the curved wall.
options.misconception: squares the density to make it look three dimensional

options.text: The cross product has length u times root 2, so it vanishes only at the tip u = 0.
The cross product has constant length, so the cone can be extended smoothly to its tip.
options.misconception: misses the vanishing factor at the apex

options.text: The cross product has length u squared, so the area integral counts the tip twice.

options.text: The cross product never vanishes, so the cone needs no special treatment at the tip.
options.misconception: claims the apex is a regular point

questions.explanation: The cross product is (-u cos v, -u sin v, u), whose length is u times root 2, vanishing only at u = 0. The tip is a single degenerate point of measure zero.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the divergence theorem in vanishing net flux
questions.stem: In the astronomer's log, explain in writing why a field such as F(x,y,z) = (x squared, y squared, minus x squared minus y squared) has zero total outward flux through every closed box, and state the role of the divergence theorem.

answer.exemplar: The divergence of the field is 2x plus 2y minus 2x minus 2y, which is zero at every point in space. The divergence theorem then rewrites the total outward flux through a closed surface as the triple integral of the divergence over the enclosed region, so that integral vanishes and the flux is zero. No special choice of box is needed, because the divergence vanishes identically rather than only on average.

questions.explanation: Since the divergence is zero everywhere, the divergence theorem gives total flux zero for any closed surface. Symmetry alone would not do this; only the vanishing divergence forces cancellation.
questions.hint: Compute the divergence before touching the surface.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a retraced chart produces a doubled area
questions.stem: Explain in the log why a spherical parametrization with the polar angle v running from 0 to 2 pi overcounts the sphere, and state how the correct area is recovered.

answer.exemplar: The surface element of a spherical chart is r squared times the sine of the polar angle, and that sine is positive on 0 to pi and negative on pi to 2 pi, so the second half of the range retraces the same surface with the opposite orientation. Taking absolute values turns the retraced part into a positive contribution, and the integral then returns twice the true area. Halving the range, or restricting v to 0 to pi, restores the correct count of 4 pi r squared.

questions.explanation: Beyond polar angle pi the chart retraces the sphere, and the absolute value turns the retracing into added area. Changing the radius cannot help; only a shorter polar range fixes the count.
questions.hint: Check what the polar angle does past pi.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an area element and a flux element are not interchangeable
questions.stem: Explain, in the terms of the astronomer's log, why the area element dS and the flux element F dot n dS are different objects and cannot be substituted for one another.

answer.exemplar: The area element dS measures how much surface a patch covers and is a nonnegative scalar with units of area, so it appears in mass and area computations. The flux element F dot n dS is signed and includes the component of the field along the unit normal, so it measures how much field crosses the patch. Because one carries a direction and the other does not, replacing one by the other changes both the sign and the size of the result.

questions.explanation: dS is a nonnegative scalar of surface extent, while F dot n dS is signed and includes the field's normal component. Swapping them drops the angle between field and normal.
questions.hint: Ask whether a sign and a direction are involved.

questions.explanation: The true wall area is 12 pi, so rows one and three are right and row two reports twice that. The shifted range in row three still sweeps the full circle exactly once.
questions.hint: Compute the true wall area 2 pi r h first.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Zero flux through a closed surface
questions.learningObjective: Connect a field's divergence to the flux through a closed surface
questions.stem: Which statement correctly connects a field's divergence to the flux through a closed surface?

options.text: Zero divergence throughout the interior forces zero total flux through the closed surface.
Zero divergence on the surface alone forces zero total flux through it.
options.misconception: weakens the hypothesis to the surface only

options.text: Positive divergence somewhere in the interior guarantees positive total flux.
options.misconception: claims a local positive divergence decides the sign

options.text: Divergence and flux are unrelated, since flux measures the field and divergence its source.
options.misconception: denies the link between divergence and flux

questions.explanation: The divergence theorem makes the flux through a closed surface equal to the integral of the divergence over the enclosed region, so zero divergence forces zero total flux.
questions.hint: The theorem turns a surface integral into a volume integral.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Estimating sheet mass from a table
questions.learningObjective: Compute a chart mass from three tabulated patches
questions.stem: The log lists three chart patches with areas 2.5, 1.5 and 4.0 square metres and average densities 18, 32 and 11 kilograms per square metre. What mass in kilograms do these entries give?
questions.explanation: The patch masses are 45, 48 and 44 kilograms, and 45 plus 48 plus 44 is 137 kilograms. The tempting average of the densities, which is 20.33, discards the information in the areas.
questions.hint: Multiply each density by its own area, then add.

questions.learningObjective: State the difference between an area element and a flux element
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the area element dS from the flux element F dot n dS on a patch of a log-drawn dome?

options.text: They are the same quantity, since both describe how much surface a patch covers.
options.misconception: treats the flux element as a pure area measure

options.text: The area element is unsigned and measures surface, while the flux element is signed and measures crossing.
The flux element is dS divided by the cosine of the angle between field and normal.
options.misconception: inverts the cosine factor in the flux formula

options.text: The area element carries a sign, and the flux element is always nonnegative.
options.misconception: assigns the sign to the wrong one of the two elements

questions.explanation: The area element measures surface extent and carries no sign, while the flux element carries the signed normal component. Swapping them mixes a mass formula with a flux formula.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two contains a direction.

questions.learningObjective: Compare fluxes on patches where area and field component trade off
questions.stem: Two patches on a log-drawn parabola have areas 2 and 5, and their normal field components are 6 and 1. Which statement about the flux through the pair is correct?

options.text: The fluxes are 12 and 5, so the larger patch contributes more because it is bigger.
options.misconception: lets the area override the field component

options.text: The fluxes cannot be compared, because the two patches lie at different angles to the field.
options.misconception: invents missing angle information to block a comparison

options.text: The fluxes are 12 and 5, so the smaller patch contributes more than twice the flux of the larger.
The fluxes are 3 and 0.2, because the field components must be divided by the areas.
options.misconception: divides component by area instead of multiplying

questions.explanation: The fluxes are 12 and 5, so the smaller patch carries more than twice as much. Area alone cannot decide the comparison when the normal components differ.
questions.hint: Multiply each area by its own normal component.
